opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot. Right now most masking strategies are fairly agnostic to what's actually in the scene. In I-JEPA, for example, we use multi-block masking: we sample a few reasonably large target blocks and a context block, and the scale and aspect ratio of those blocks were chosen so the targets tend to cover semantically meaningful regions. That works surprisingly well, but it's a heuristic. We're hoping a block is big enough to capture part of an object, not making sure it does.

Ideally an object-aware approach would mask at the level of entities instead of arbitrary patches. If you hide an entire object, or a coherent part of one, the model can't solve the prediction task by interpolating low-level texture from neighboring pixels. It has to reason about what's plausibly there given the rest of the scene. That pushes the representation toward semantics, which is what we want.

The catch is that I wouldn't want this to depend on supervised segmentation or human-annotated object masks. That brings back a lot of the hand-crafted priors and labeling cost that self-supervised learning is trying to get away from. So I'd want the notion of "objectness" to emerge from the learning process itself. One way is to bootstrap it: the model's own representations, or the attention structure in the target encoder, give you a rough grouping of patches into regions, and you use that to decide what to mask. As the representations improve, the masks get more object-like, which in turn makes the prediction task more semantic. It's a self-reinforcing loop, though you have to be careful it doesn't collapse into something trivial.

Video is where this gets especially interesting, because motion is a strong free signal for objectness. Things that move together tend to belong together. So you could use temporal coherence to define regions and mask an object across a span of frames, a kind of spatiotemporal tube that follows the object instead of a fixed spatial location. Then the model has to predict where the object went and how it changed, not just copy from the adjacent frame, which is a very easy shortcut in video if you're not careful with masking.

The last piece is that I'd want the prediction to happen in representation space, not pixel space. If you mask out an object and ask the model to reconstruct its exact pixels, you're asking it to spend capacity on details that are inherently unpredictable, like the exact texture or lighting. Predicting the abstract representation of the masked object lets the model capture what it is and where it is without hallucinating every pixel. So, in short: mask meaningful entities, discover them without labels, use motion in video, and predict in an abstract space.

r001.rationale: It proposes masking entities and discovering them from the model’s own representations or attention, without relying on a pretrained object detector.

r002.rationale: It says objectness should emerge from learning and describes using learned representations to group patches into regions for masking.

r003.rationale: It mentions avoiding collapse into trivial masks, but does not identify object-detector quality as a bottleneck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a great question, and it gets at something we spent a lot of time thinking about. If you look at the way masking is typically done in approaches like masked autoencoders, or even in our earlier I-JEPA work, the masks are essentially random. You take the image or the video, you chop it into patches, and you drop out some fraction of them, maybe in random blocks, maybe at random locations, and then the model has to predict what's missing.

And that works surprisingly well, but if you think about it, it's a bit of a strange learning signal. If I randomly mask out, say, half the pixels of a cat, the model can often fill in what's missing just by looking at the local texture around the mask boundary. It's a kind of interpolation problem. You're not really forcing the model to learn what a cat is, you're forcing it to learn that fur continues to look like fur.

So the way I'd want an object-aware approach to work is: the masking should be aligned with the semantic structure of the scene. Instead of dropping out random patches, you'd drop out an entire object, or an entire part of an object, or in video, an object's full trajectory through time. Then the prediction task becomes much more interesting. You can't solve it by local interpolation anymore. To predict what's in that masked region, the model has to reason about the rest of the scene. There's a person here, they're reaching toward the table, so there's probably something on the table they're interacting with. That's the kind of inference we actually want representations to support.

Now, the hard part, of course, is that you don't have object annotations in self-supervised learning. That's the whole point. So there's a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem. You'd like to mask objects, but you don't know where the objects are yet. The way I'd want this to work is in a kind of bootstrapping loop. The model's own representations, even early in training, carry some notion of what regions belong together. You can cluster those features, or look at the attention patterns, and get rough segments for free. Then you use those segments to define your masks, and the better the masks get, the better the representations get, and so on.

In video specifically, I think this is actually easier than in images, because motion gives you a very strong, cheap signal for objectness. Things that move together tend to be the same object. So you can get reasonably good spatiotemporal masks just from motion cues, and then you mask out the whole tube and ask the model to predict the representation of that tube from the surrounding context. That pushes the model to learn things like object permanence, how objects interact, what happens when something goes behind an occluder, and these are exactly the properties you'd want from a world model.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that I'd want this to happen in representation space, not in pixel space. If you ask the model to reconstruct the pixels of the masked object, you're spending a lot of capacity on predicting exactly where every whisker is, which is both hard and not very useful. Whereas if you're predicting an abstract representation of the masked region, the model can be uncertain about low-level details and still get credit for having the right high-level understanding. Combining that abstraction with object-aligned masking, I think, is where you start to get representations that genuinely capture the structure of the world rather than just its statistics.

r001.rationale: It proposes deriving masks from the model’s own representations or video motion cues, without requiring a pretrained object detector.

r002.rationale: It describes a self-supervised bootstrapping loop that uses clustered features, attention patterns, or motion to find object regions without annotations.

r003.rationale: It identifies the lack of object annotations as a challenge, but does not identify object-detector quality as a potential bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I’d want the masking to operate at the level of objects rather than just randomly selecting patches. So, imagine a video of someone picking up a cup. Ideally, you could mask the cup and ask the model to predict a representation of what’s missing from the surrounding scene and the action.

The challenge is making sure the model can’t solve that by looking at a tiny visible piece of the cup, or copying it from the neighboring frame. You’d want the masking to be consistent enough across space and time that the model actually has to understand something about the scene and how it evolves.

And ideally, those object regions would emerge from the learning process itself. You wouldn’t want to need a labeled dataset or a separate, supervised object detector just to decide what to mask.

r001.rationale: It says object regions should emerge from learning without a separate supervised object detector, communicating detector-free object-aware masking.

r002.rationale: It says object regions should emerge from learning without labeled data, expressing unsupervised discovery for masking.

r003.rationale: It discusses leakage from visible object parts and neighboring frames, but does not identify object-detector quality as a bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
Ideally, I’d want the masking to operate at the level of objects rather than just randomly selecting patches. If you mask a small part of an object, the model can often fill it in using nearby texture or color. It doesn’t necessarily need to understand what’s in the scene.

If you could mask an entire object, then the model would have to use the surrounding context to predict what belongs there. In video, you could extend that idea over time, so you’re not simply finding the same object in an adjacent frame and copying it over. You’d want the prediction task to require some understanding of the object and how it relates to the rest of the scene.

The tricky part is getting those object-level masks without already having a system that knows where the objects are. Ideally, that structure would emerge through learning, without requiring someone to annotate all the objects for you.

r001.rationale: It proposes object-level masking and says the masks should be learned without an existing system that already knows object locations.

r002.rationale: It says object structure should emerge through learning without requiring object annotations.

r003.rationale: It notes the challenge of obtaining object masks, but does not identify object-detector quality as a potential bottleneck.
